https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ceq8.text: Image source, DFFE Image caption, Staff at the National Zoological Garden in Pretoria have been looking after the eggs and hatchlings By Hafsa Khalil Published 30 minutes ago Fifty eggs suspected to be those of endangered parrots were intercepted at South Africa's main airport in Johannesburg last Thursday - and some of them have now hatched. A 50-year-old Thai national was arrested for allegedly attempting to smuggle them in a "homemade incubator bag" carried as hand luggage, according to the Department of Forestry, Fisheries and the Environment (DFFE). Many of the rescued eggs have successfully hatched, with the chicks now receiving "intensive" care to "maximise their chances of survival", it added. If convicted, the suspected wildlife trafficker faces a fine of up to 10m rand ($626,000, Â£461,000) or up to 10 years in prison, or both. Initial investigations suggest the eggs belong to a parrot species protected under the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (Cites). The arrest followed a joint operation by the DFFE, the Green Scorpions - a specialised environmental enforcement unit - and various divisions of the police. Environment Minister David Maynier has congratulated all the agencies involved, saying "illegal wildlife trafficking can only be challenged by a co-ordinated defence of our natural heritage". He particularly thanked the dedicated staff at the National Zoological Garden in the capital, Pretoria, "who have been working tirelessly to incubate the seized eggs and provide specialised care to the hatchlings". Last Thursday's arrest follows that of a 23-year-old Thai citizen in July, also caught at Johannesburg's OR Tambo International Airport, who was attempting to smuggle 418 parrot eggs. The arrests highlighted the growing sophistication of transnational wildlife trafficking networks and reinforced "the importance of co-ordinated, intelligence-led law enforcement efforts", the DFFE said. The illegal collection and trafficking of parrot eggs posed "a serious threat to wild bird populations and animal welfare", it added. Officials explained that such eggs were often smuggled in improvised incubators and in conditions that endangered the welfare of developing embryos and hatchlings. Wildlife trafficking remains a major threat in South Africa, one of the world's most biodiverse countries, with criminal networks frequently targeting animals such as elephants and pangolins, for sale on the international black market. To combat the threat, the country adopted a new strategy six years ago to strengthen collaboration between government institutions, law enforcement agencies, conservation authorities, customs officials, prosecutors and international partners to dismantle criminal networks involved in the illicit wildlife trade. Photograph: Francisco Seco/AP View image in fullscreen Local people watch firefighters go to work after a Russian drone attack struck a residential building in Kyiv this week. Photograph: Francisco Seco/AP Europe Europe would not be able to sustain war of attrition with Russia, defence officials say Security experts fear Putin may be winning hybrid war with the west amid rise of pro-Kremlin, far-right parties Patrick Wintour in Rome Sat 5 Sep 2026 07.00 EDT Last modified on Sat 5 Sep 2026 07.02 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Defence planners working with Nato fear that if war broke out with Russia , Europe could not currently sustain a prolonged war of attrition owing to a public lack of war readiness, a conference on the future of European military coordination heard this week. The pessimism reflects concern that Russia may be winning a so-called hybrid war with Europe , weakening the options available to Nato war planners in the event of military conflict. The surge in support for the populist forces in Europe’s main military states is also endangering proposals for a group of five European countries, including the UK, to take on a new coordination role as the US prepares to reduce its commitments to the conventional defence of Europe. Defence officials, speaking at a forum convened by the Munich Security Conference (MSC), the leading security foundation, said the European public may not have the appetite for a prolonged war, requiring Nato to focus its plans on a relatively quick conflict. One recent British cabinet member admitted the west had been “crap” at educating its public about the scale of the hybrid conflict with Russia. Another UK diplomat claimed successive British prime ministers had done nothing to explain the scale of the threat. They said this had left ministers locked in an unenviable task of persuading unprepared voters to cut welfare spending to fund defence. “The level of the debate has been at that of a kindergarten,” the UK diplomat admitted. View image in fullscreen Russia’s president, Vladimir Putin, takes part in a wreath laying ceremony in Moscow earlier this year. Photograph: Maxim Shipenkov/Reuters The private criticism has been fuelled by the UK government’s inability to adopt a call in its 2025 strategic defence review to launch a national conversation on the scale of the security threat facing Europe and to build national resilience. A second diplomat said the collapse of the cold war dividing line with Russia had left Moscow free to exploit the anxieties of European publics on the left and the right. The remarks reveal a wider concern in senior European politicians that they may be losing the so-called hybrid war with Russia , and this may be reflected in rightwing populist surges next year in Poland, France and Italy. Most populist parties, including Germany’s Alternative für Deutschland (AfD), are sympathetic to Russia and want an end to the Ukraine conflict. The MSC discussion – held under rules forbidding identification of the speaker – was given added urgency by the German government this week blaming Russia for an attempted drone attack on Leipzig airport last month. One of the suspected culprits in the attack on 4 August, where an armed drone exploded, has been identified as a Belarusian citizen with a Russian passport who appears to have entered Europe using an Italian tourist visa. The MSC, an independent but influential foundation, has been promoting the idea of the five main European military powers working much more closely: one means of bringing the UK, outside the EU, to the centre of European defence planning. Decisions in Washington on its troop deployments that could effectively leave Europe in charge of its own conventional defences are expected in the next few months. But the scale of hybrid war and the potential impact of next year’s elections, as well as the surge by the AfD in Germany , on plans for a stronger European defence coordination was described at the conference as “the elephant in the room”. Deadly escalation in Black Sea attacks prompts fears of even higher food prices Read more One proposal is for the EU to publish a collective statement on the Russian threat that the populist forces would be challenged to accept or decline. The E5 group of European defence ministers already meet regularly, but they are at the early stages of agreeing of how to jointly procure capabilities such as integrated air and missile defence, deep precision strike and space-based early warning systems that are all currently provided mostly by the US. “Europe is stagnating at a time when the external threats were assuming a dimension which is really very serious. These are really huge and existential challenges requiring greater integration in defence,” said Wolfgang Ischinger, the chair of the MSC. He argued the E5 grouping offers a way of including all the European countries with substantial defence industrial capacity and may later be able to incorporate Ukraine in the context of a truce since Kyiv now has the largest and strongest army in Europe. Advocates of the E5 insist it will neither duplicate nor underline Nato, but fears were expressed that the US would nevertheless block a stronger European pillar inside Nato. “The US are better at talking about burden shifting than power sharing,” said one diplomat. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every day Sign up to Headlines Europe A digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week day after newsletter promotion Italy is one of the E5 states most concerned about the impact of Russia’s hybrid warfare on its domestic politics as Giorgia Meloni’s rightwing administration – which has governed more moderately than many expected, and cultivated a pro-Ukraine image abroad – becomes its longest-running since the second world war. The Italian foreign minister, Antonio Tajani, warned Italy was suffering daily cyber-attacks, adding it was not immune from potential Russian interference in next year’s national elections, the first time an Italian politicians has warned the election may be manipulated. View image in fullscreen Italy’s foreign minister, Antonio Tajani, has warned of Russia meddling in his country’s elections next year. Photograph: Mohamed Hossam/EPA “There are many ways to wage hybrid warfare, it is not done using bombs, planes or tanks,” the minister said. Italy’s defence minister, Guido Crosetto, one of Meloni’s closest political allies, has said it was stupid not to recognise the level of Russian interference. He warned this summer at the Nato summit in Ankara: “We don’t have the antibodies and we’re penetrable: analyse bots and you’ll see it. The increase occurred thanks to social media.” His doubts have grown given Moscow’s ability to operate across so many domains, including social media, AI, cybersecurity, databases and critical infrastructure. On Tuesday, he said the Russian threat was growing all the time. Crosetto also said he recognises Russia is exploiting real problems such as low wages, and so attributing government unpopularity to Russian disinformation risks misidentifying a malaise afflicting western societies, including a general weariness with the cost of the war in Ukraine, In Italy, Roberto Vannacci, the leader of the far-right Futuro Nazionale who has challenged the stability of Meloni’s coalition , is widely seen as the most probable carrier of the Russian message in the coming election, that could come as early as April. Speaking before the investigation into whether his party represents a revival of fascism, Vannacci gloried in the criticism. “Just discovered that I am a ‘Manchurian candidate’ sent by the Russian federation to complain about the unaffordable petrol prices in my country Italy,” he said. “Forgive me, but I still find it hard to accept the idea that dissent from Brussels’ orthodoxy is now, in practical terms, tantamount to disloyalty towards the west.” In an attempt to shift perceptions so Ukraine is seen not as a financial burden but rather as teaching Europe modern warfare, Crosetto has recruited the former Ukraine defence minister Mykhailo Fedorov as his unpaid adviser for innovation. Ischinger praised the decision, describing Ukraine as possessing the best equipped and most modern army in Europe. In Ukraine, 200,000 drones are being built each month, with the goal of producing more than 7m by 2026. To support this growth, 500 small and medium-sized companies have sprung up, assembling drones even in small workshops, using mostly Chinese components. Beállítom Hétfőn délelőtt nyújtotta be a Pénzügyminiszter a parlamentnek az üzemanyag-áremelkedésre tekintettel nyújtott támogatásokkal összefüggő intézkedésekről és kapcsolódó törvények módosításáról szóló törvénymódosító javaslatot . Ebben foglalták össze azokat a módosításokat, amik ahhoz szükségesek, hogy be tudják vezetni a havi ötezer forintos dízeltámogatást , amit az üzemanyagárak emelkedésének kompenzálására talált ki a kormány. De a javaslatban nemcsak ez szerepel, hanem a dohánytermékek jövedéki adójának jelentős emelése is. A kormány kérte azt is, hogy a javaslatot kivételes eljárásban tárgyalja meg a parlament. Ez azt jelenti, hogy a hétfőn reggel benyújtott módosításokról a tervek szerint kedden este már szavazni is fog az országgyűlés. Mivel a kormánypártnak többsége van, várhatóan el is fogják fogadni. A kivételes eljárást azzal indokolták, hogy a módosításhoz kiemelt nemzeti érdek fűződik. A dízeltámogatásra vonatkozó szabályok már a kihirdetést követő másnap életbe is lépnének. A dohánytermékekre vonatkozó adóemelés azonban csak november 1-jén lép hatályba, ha elfogadják a törvényt. A javaslatban nem indokolták, hogy miért ebben a javaslatban rejtették el az adóemelést, ami jelentősen drágíthatja a dohánytermékeket. A javaslat szerint ugyanis a cigaretta esetében például az eddig ezer szálanként legalább 47 140 forintos jövedéki adó novembertől ezer szálanként legalább 59 800 forint lesz. Ez azt jelenti, hogy egy doboz 20 szálas cigaretta után eddig legalább 943 forint jövedéki adót kellett fizetni, novembertől viszont 1196 forint lesz a minimum adómérték. Azaz egy doboz cigaretta adója legalább 253 forinttal fog nőni. https://www.express.co.uk/news/uk/224623.text: Home News UK Budapest city skyline and Danube River (Image: Getty Images/iStockphoto) A pair of British policemen have been arrested after an alleged “sun and sex orgy” involving 15 colleagues from the same station took place during a group summer holiday. A female officer alleged that during the “wild” sex party one of the men forcefully removed her from a room by grabbing her arm before taking her to his own room, accusing him of assault. There is no suggestion he tried to have sex with her, however the woman has alleged that she was also sexually assaulted by a second male colleague. The trip to Hungarian capital of Budapest involved 15 off-duty Met officers who went on holiday together and it is understood that some of them were already sexually involved with each other prior to the “orgy”. Article continues below ADVERTISEMENT Edinburgh crash LIVE: Huge 999 response to A8 near major airport after horror collision Portsmouth LIVE: Protesters clash with riot police after '140 migrants arrive on dinghy' New Scotland Yard (Image: Tayfun Salci/ZUMA Press Wire/REX/Shutterstock) The group of young officers had been staying at a large house in Budapest booked via Airbnb in June this year. Investigators have been told that during a boozy night out several officers began having sex with one another before the female constable alleges she was assaulted. The Met has confirmed that the two constables have been arrested, bailed and suspended from duty. Sources have claimed that Scotland Yard is “deeply embarrassed” by the so-called “sex party” as it carries out an internal investigation alongside the criminal probe. Article continues below ADVERTISEMENT One person with knowledge of the incident told The Sun: “It shows just how deeply embarrassed the Met are by this. It beggars belief that this could happen. “An official internal probe is trying to establish exactly what happened on this trip.” Budapest, Hungary - Beautiful aerial skyline view of Budapest at sunrise with Szechenyi Chain Bridge (Image: Getty Images/iStockphoto) Another insider claimed several police sergeants had been on holiday as part of the group and that they are now being quizzed over “how they let these scenes go on”. The source said: “It is one thing to say that what goes on while on tour should stay on tour, but these were apparently wild scenes which have led to criminal complaints.” They added that there “seems to have been a complete lack of supervision” by the more senior officers, which the Met's Directorate of Professional Standards is now focusing its investigation on. A Met Police spokesman said: “Two serving officers have been arrested following an investigation by the Met's Directorate of Professional Standards. “One officer, attached to Central North Command, was arrested on Monday, 31 August on suspicion of assault. “A second officer, attached to the same command, was arrested on Thursday, 3 September on suspicion of sexual assault. “The incidents are reported to have taken place in Budapest in June 2026. Both officers were bailed and have been suspended from duty, and enquiries continue into what is a complex investigation. “All allegations of criminality or misconduct by officers are treated with the utmost seriousness.” Comments Unavailable Sorry, we are unable to accept comments about this article at the moment. https://www.theguardian.com/law/2026/oct.text: Luke Ings (left) and Liam Bennett were jailed as teenagers. Composite: ITV Meridian View image in fullscreen Luke Ings (left) and Liam Bennett were jailed as teenagers. Composite: ITV Meridian UK criminal justice Two men serving indefinite jail sentences freed after two decades Convicted pair, plus third man released in August, have IPPs replaced after serving much longer than minimum terms Rajeev Syal Home affairs editor Wed 7 Oct 2026 15.16 EDT First published on Wed 7 Oct 2026 12.56 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Two men jailed with indefinite sentences for public protection (IPPs) have been freed after each serving about two decades in custody despite receiving minimum terms of two years or less. A high court judge and a magistrate hearing an appeal after a review by the Criminal Cases Review Commission (CCRC) told Luke Ings and Liam Bennett they would be freed, and also replaced an indeterminate sentence given to a third man, James Ward. Ward, who was freed in 2017 after serving 10 years more than his one-year minimum and was later recalled to prison, was also in court, sitting in the public gallery to see his original sentence replaced. Relatives of Ings and Bennett hugged in the public gallery at Wolverhampton crown court on Wednesday as Mr Justice Choudhury told them the IPPs had been “cancelled”. Choudhury said Bennett would instead be sentenced to four years and 264 days, Ward to two years, and Ings to 42 months with a 30-month extended licence. All three men’s original sentences were quashed and replaced after they argued that judges had wrongly found them to be dangerous or had not considered alternative sentences. Choudhury, sitting with the magistrate Norma Grant, told the appellants: “You have already spent considerably longer than those [replacement] sentences in custody. The effect is that you, Mr Bennett, and you, Mr Ings, will be entitled to release without further supervision, and you, Mr Ward, will no longer be subject to supervision.” The ruling came after the CCRC referred the cases of the three men back to the crown court to review minimum terms imposed on them by judges in Wolverhampton, Reading and Leicester respectively in 2006 and 2007. Bennett and Ings, now both 38, were 17 when they committed offences that led to them being classed as dangerous offenders and given indeterminate sentences with respective minimum terms of 24 months and 21 months in 2007 and 2006. Bennett was originally sentenced at Wolverhampton crown court in May 2007 after being found guilty of reckless arson for setting fire to items in the loft space of an empty council property, and admitting criminal damage and burglary. Ings was sentenced to detention for public protection after appearing at East Berkshire youth court in March 2006 and admitting offences including a robbery in an underpass and an assault on a teenager in a fast food outlet. Ward, now 41, was 21 when he was given a one-year minimum sentence in 2006 at Leicester crown court for arson and criminal damage. He admitted arson – after setting fire to items in his prison cell while serving time for assault – and was released in 2017, but was later recalled to prison and remained in custody until August this year. Muin Boase, representing Bennett, successfully argued that the judge who sentenced him in 2007 did not give proper weight to his youth, lack of maturity and capacity to change after a difficult childhood. In its ruling, the appeal court said there had been no proper basis for the original finding of dangerousness. Detention for public protection and imprisonment for public protection (DPP and IPP) sentences were abolished in 2012, having been made available to tackle offenders considered a significant risk to the public in 2005. The law was changed to stop courts handing out IPP sentences after warnings that they were being applied too widely, but the abolition was not retrospective, meaning many prisoners serving such sentences are still behind bars. The government has faced calls to take action on IPP jail terms, with the former justice secretary Ken Clarke saying last month that ministers should not to be too cautious. His comments came a week after the current justice secretary, Alex Norris, told MPs that the government planned to bring forward legislation to end IPP sentences “once and for all” by the end of this parliament. More than 2,000 prisoners remain held indefinitely under IPP sentences, with 99% past their original tariff and 80% having served 10 years or more. https://socialistworker.co.uk/teach-your.text: By Judy Cox Downloading PDF. Please wait... Sunday 25 October 2026 Issue 3029 Teach Yourself Marxism Are institutions independent from capitalism? The institutions of civil society reflect something deeper than the interests of the ruling class By Judy Cox Downloading PDF. Please wait... Sunday 25 October 2026 Issue 3029 Why have institutions like churches covered up abuse for centuries? (Photo: WikipediaCommons) The Cornell 7 case has once again propelled institutional sexual abuse into the spotlight. Members of Chi Phi frat house at Cornell University sexually assaulted Jane Doe. The university tried to hush it up. Why do respected institutions choose to protect their reputation at the expense of survivors of abuse? Italian Marxist Antonio Gramsci distinguished between the institutions of the state and the institutions of what he called civil society. Civil society is made up of voluntary organisations which exist between state institutions and the privatised family. State institutions—the police, the courts, prisons, the armed forces—systematically use violence to reinforce hierarchies of control. The ruling class exerts its ideological influence through civil society—the Church, the media, leisure and sport. The intuitions of the state and of civil society reinforce each other. They also reproduce hierarchies, those with influence can coerce and silence those with less power. The Protestant and Catholic Churches have harboured abusers and exploited people to organise cover ups. Decades before Jeffrey Epstein recruited politicians, CEOs and celebrities to his grooming gang, there was the Kincora Boys’ Home in Belfast. “Housefathers” there sexually abused boys at the home for 20 years before it was exposed in 1980. British intelligence protected senior figures from the military and judiciary who were involved in the abuse. Jimmy Saville used his status at the BBC to abuse hundreds of children. Saville was protected by BBC executives, government ministers and his friendship with the then prince Charles. They ignored rumours about his paedophilia and necrophilia to bask in his celebrity. He was only exposed after his death in 2011. An inquiry into the scandals of Kincora and Saville found that political and religious institutions “regularly put their own reputations or political interests before child protection”. Institutions such as the BBC are formally independent of the state. But they reflect and reinforce social inequalities. The rich create and sustain institutions and networks that protect each other. Their schools and clubs are based on excluding, bullying and abusing others. This trains them to be brutal and ruthless “leaders”. But the institutions of civil society reflect something deeper than the interests of the ruling class. Capitalism alienates us all from what makes us human—our capacity to work collectively to produce what we need. We attribute human powers to inanimate objects. The things we create come to dominate us. Karl Marx observed that under capitalism, “It seems as if the thing itself possesses the ability, the virtue, to establish production relations”, rather than the workers who produce the thing. What happens in relation to commodities generalises across society. It appears that some mysterious force called “the market” causes prices to rise and fall. The extension of the state and the development of huge corporations have created sprawling bureaucracies. These bureaucracies take on an existence independent of their original function. They become an end in themselves. Hungarian Marxist George Lukacs described how these institutions generate a “bureaucratic ‘conscientiousness’”. The worker in the bureaucracy develops a “sense of responsibility” towards the institution that employs them. The bureaucracy itself becomes the important thing, not the service it was set up to provide for people. This creates what Lukacs called a “ghostly objectivity” in which institutions appear to represent an objective force for stability and order. Making the institution work, and protecting its reputation, becomes the primary objective for those enslaved to an institution. But human action creates institutions and human action can tear them down. And we have the collective power to challenge the sick system which dehumanises us all.
